summary: Project Hail Mary Thumbs Up built a lunar navigation map that helps mission planners choose where to place solar arrays on the Moon while keeping a line of sight to Earth. Using a lunar elevation map, we calculate the horizon angle for every location in each direction. We then compare it against the Sun's position over a full lunar day to find the percentage of time each spot is lit, and against Earth's position to find where terrain blocks communication. The result is a set of maps showing sunlight exposure and Earth visibility, and a combined map highlighting the best sites. Near the lunar poles the Sun stays very low, so even small ridges cast long shadows, which makes careful site selection essential. Our approach, written in Python, finds sites with strong power and reliable communication, and it can scale to higher-resolution terrain data. In our test area, the best site receives 100% sunlight and identifies optimal ridges for continuous lunar surface operations.
details:
Welcome to Project Hail Mary Thumbs Up‘s Lunar Navigation Details!


What It Does & How It Works

Our tool takes a lunar elevation map and, for every location, calculates how high the surrounding terrain blocks the sky in each direction (the horizon angle). Comparing those horizon profiles against the real positions of the Sun and Earth over a full lunar day reveals what percentage of the time each spot is lit and what percentage of the time it maintains a direct line of sight to Earth. A combined map then highlights the optimal sites for solar arrays that also require uninterrupted communication with Earth.

What about its Benefits & Intended Impact?

Mission planners can compare candidate landing and base sites quickly and select locations that balance strong solar power with reliable communications. This matters most near the lunar poles, where the Sun stays very low on the horizon and even small ridges cast long, persistent shadows.

What are the Tools, Coding Languages & Data Used
  • ﻿﻿Languages & Engines: Python, GDScript, and Godot Engine
  • ﻿﻿Python Libraries:
    NumPy, rasterio, matplotlib, and Skyfield
  • ﻿﻿Astronomical & Terrain Data: NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris data (accounting for lunar libration) and NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA Digital Elevation Model
    (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ ).
Creativity

Rather than running separate models for power and communications, we use a single unified horizon-angle test for both sunlight exposure and Earth line-of-sight, scoring candidate sites on both criteria simultaneously. We also paired Python geospatial data processing with Godot and GDScript for interactive visualization.
